maths_errors.text: If the question says 'without replacement' or 'given that', the events are not independent.
maths_errors.correction: The words 'given that' do not make events dependent. A question can say 'given that' about independent events, and then P(A | B) = P(A). For example, two dice: P(second shows 6 | first shows 6) = 1/6. Only the without-replacement part of the statement holds in general.

maths_errors.text: applying the simple multiplication rule P(A) × P(B) when the question involves 'without replacement' or a condition.
maths_errors.correction: P(A) × P(B) is wrong only when the events are dependent. 'A condition' in the question does not on its own make the rule wrong. When events are dependent, the correct rule is P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A).

Interpretation is not taught. The lesson never explains what a conditional probability tells you, and never compares P(A | B) with P(A), for example to judge whether knowing B changes the likelihood of A.

above_gcse.text: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B)
above_gcse.why: The specification requires conditional probability through representations (two-way tables, tree diagrams, Venn diagrams, expected frequencies), not the formal formula. This is A-level style. It is also never used with probabilities in the lesson, only with counts, so it may confuse more than help.

density.text: Knowing extra information restricts the sample space — you no longer consider all possible outcomes, only those consistent with what you've been told.
density.why: 'Sample space' is used without being defined, and the sentence carries two ideas joined by a dash.

density.text: For example, if you know a card drawn is red, you're no longer considering all 52 cards — only the 26 red ones, so every probability recalculated from that point must use 26 as the denominator, not 52.
density.why: One sentence carries the example, the restriction and the rule about the denominator.

density.text: B is the condition that restricts your sample space, so you divide by P(B) to rescale.
density.why: 'Rescale' is not explained. The reason for dividing by P(B) is asserted, not shown.

density.text: P(A | B) is read as 'the probability of A given B' — given that B has already happened, what is the probability that A also happens?
density.why: The whole field is a long paragraph packing notation, meaning, rescaling, a plain-English restatement and the count version together. It is hard to take in on one read.
